item.title: An FBI arrest revives fears that U.S. tech companies are hiring spies
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
On paper, Abdulrahman Alfozan seemed like an ideal candidate for one of Silicon Valley's most coveted artificial intelligence jobs. The Saudi national attended the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and landed an engineering job at Meta, according to his LinkedIn page and online records. Alfozan later secured a green card, spoke enthusiastically on a podcast about his Silicon Valley career and was invited to speak at Stanford University, all while working as a part-time partner at a venture capital fund dedicated to expanding the tech ecosystem in the Middle East. He had lived in the United States for more than a decade when he scored a mid-level role at OpenAI last year. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. But Alfozan's arrest on Tuesday for allegedly planting a recording device in OpenAI's headquarters has ignited a fierce debate about the potential risks of Silicon Valley's international workforce - employees who often hail from nations seeking to rival the AI superpower status of the U.S. Foreign nationals have long formed the backbone of the American tech industry, helping U.S. companies surpass their would-be international rivals. Last week, President Donald Trump awarded national medals to six tech titans for their contributions to American innovation. Five of them, including Google co-founder Sergey Brin and SpaceX founder Elon Musk, were immigrants. As countries battle to dominate AI, some top executives in Silicon Valley have argued that winning what they see as an existential arms race requires aggressively recruiting even more top talent from around the world. As recently as April, Katrina Mulligan, a senior member of OpenAI's national security team, called for an "accelerated pathway to citizenship" for such workers, referring to foreign hires as a "national strategic asset" at an event on Capitol Hill. She estimated that a significant number of OpenAI's employees were not U.S. citizens, including Chinese nationals. Just half of the 300 top AI researchers in the world, she said, were American. Other industry leaders - as well as some lawmakers - have long accused top-tier tech companies with many foreign workers of disadvantaging Americans and being breeding grounds for Chinese espionage. Palmer Luckey, CEO of weapons maker Anduril, and venture capitalist Shaun Maguire of Sequoia Capital took to X on Wednesday to revisit arguments that the industry should focus on hiring U.S. citizens. "Silicon Valley has operated with maximum openness and maximum naivete toward foreign tradecraft," Maguire wrote. Alfozan's arrest and the debates it has re-ignited show how the AI boom has sharpened a fundamental tension in Silicon Valley: American firms must recruit from a global pool of talent while also protecting innovations that governments around the world are racing to develop or obtain for themselves. The situation is getting even more complicated as competition intensifies, said Chris McGuire, senior fellow for China and emerging technologies at the Council on Foreign Relations, and a member of the National Security Council during the Biden administration. "This technology is too powerful for [countries beyond the U.S. and China] to ignore, and the quickest and cheapest way to advance capabilities is to steal it," he added. Arrests and convictions are relatively rare compared to the large numbers of foreign workers at U.S. tech firms. Much discussion focuses on workers from China, whose government has pledged to overtake the U.S. in AI. American intelligence agencies have long warned U.S. tech firms that they are targets of Chinese intelligence services. "There are any number of countries that would want to know about the internal workings and future plans of OpenAI and its competitors," said Ryan Fedasiuk, a fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, a Washington think tank. A spokesperson for OpenAI declined to comment. The company said in a statement late Tuesday that Alfozan's employment had been terminated. (The Washington Post has a content partnership with OpenAI.) In recent years, the Middle East has sought to become a major force in American technology. Funding from the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia have helped to fuel the costly AI boom, and billion-dollar investments often come with reciprocal obligations for U.S. AI companies to build advanced tech in the region. Last year the Trump administration gave both countries access to some of the most advanced AI chips in the U.S. - reversing the Biden administration's more cautious stance. Alfozan has not been charged with foreign espionage and the U.S. government has not said whether he was acting alone or as an agent of a foreign government. But there are signs that the U.S. government is exploring the latter possibility, McGuire said. The Department of Justice's press release about the incident says that the National Security Division's Counterintelligence and Export Control section, whose responsibility includes prosecuting spies, is assisting with the case. National Intelligence Director Jay Clayton, in his statements on the case, said U.S. intelligence was committed to protecting America from "foreign threats." A Washington-based Middle East expert, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to avoid incurring wrath from Saudi Arabia, said he believed the Saudi government was almost certainly involved in some way. "No one does this, not even for patriotism, without getting paid," said the person. And money would not be distributed without agreement by the Saudi royal court, he said. The Saudis lag behind their regional rival, the United Arab Emirates, in artificial intelligence development, he added. A former CIA officer with extensive experience in the Middle East, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive internal Saudi dynamics, said that Saudi nationals working in Silicon Valley are celebrated back home. It's a "huge thing" for the Saudi government, said the former agency official, because Riyadh wants to build its own native technology talent base. By working at a prominent Silicon Valley firm, you become a "big dog," said the former officer. Alfozan, his wife and a third family member had booked one-way tickets to travel on Oct. 12 from San Francisco to Saudi Arabia via Istanbul, according to a motion filed by the government Oct. 8 in federal court and unsealed Wednesday. The former OpenAI employee's public biography shows links to the Saudi government. Prince Khalid bin Bader al Saud, a member of the Saudi royal family, is a partner at RAED Ventures, which also lists Alfozan as a partner. The firm's X account has posted photos of partners hosting several high-ranking Saudi officials at events. RAED did not respond to a request for comment. In a podcast interview posted last month, Alfozan said he met Saudi Arabia's crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, before he became the country's top leader during one of the prince's trips to Silicon Valley. Bin Salman inspired Alfozan to stay in Silicon Valley and grow his skills so that he could use them when he eventually returned to Saudi Arabia, he said in the interview. At OpenAI on Wednesday, employees continued tense conversations about the political implications of the arrest for immigrant workers, two OpenAI employees said, speaking on the condition of anonymity to describe internal discussions. The Justice Department said Tuesday that OpenAI determined the device was likely planted on Sept. 28. A company spokesman said it was found in a security sweep two days later. The arrest triggered a discussion on OpenAI's internal Slack messaging platform among employees about whether the incident might increase pressure from the Trump administration on OpenAI to not hire foreign nationals, said one of the people. In March, Emil Michael, the Pentagon's chief technology officer, wrote in court papers that AI developer Anthropic's reliance on staff with ties to China was among the concerns that fueled the Defense Department's conflict with the AI company. Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment. Lawmakers have been seeking to tighten the government's oversight of the security risks faced by AI companies. In September, Sens. Jim Banks (R-Indiana) and Kirsten Gillibrand (D-New York) introduced a bill that would require AI companies that do business with the Pentagon to tell officials how they vet personnel and manage threats posed by insiders, and to report incidents of suspected espionage. "While we await more details, this incident underscores the need for a commonsense notification framework for AI contractors to alert the Pentagon to a range of security threats," Gillibrand said in a statement Wednesday. Tensions inside the tech industry over hiring and security practices spilled out openly Wednesday on X. Silicon Valley insiders recounted stories of stiff security within tech firms due to concerns about espionage from both commercial companies and foreign governments, in recent years. Many companies have stepped up their security practices during the recent AI boom, often using the technology itself to speed up their understanding of strange behavior and patterns, according to Ryan Schonfeld, cofounder and CEO of HiveWatch, a startup that helps tech companies secure their facilities against insider threats. "What used to be considered very sophisticated ... now is par for the course," he said. item.title: 9 FBI employees who investigated Trump sue over firings and allege retaliation
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Washington — Nine former FBI employees sued the bureau on Thursday, saying they were unlawfully terminated merely for working on former special counsel Jack Smith's investigation into President Trump's retention of classified records after his first term in the White House. The former special agents, intelligence analysts and staff operation specialists worked on counterintelligence investigations and were fired over the course of two days in February 2026 — just as the United States and Israel were set to begin military strikes against Iran. The nine plaintiffs represent the latest in a growing number of former FBI agents and other personnel who have filed lawsuits against the Justice Department and the bureau after they were abruptly terminated. Many of the fired employees worked on matters that displeased Mr. Trump and his allies. The plaintiffs "were unlawfully terminated not for any cause or any legitimate reason, but only to satisfy the President's personal vendetta," the lawsuit alleged. "The firings did not follow any internal investigation or disciplinary process within the FBI, and Plaintiffs were not given any notice, a hearing, or an opportunity to appeal. Instead, Patel claimed to rely solely upon 'Article II' to support the firings," the suit said, referring to FBI Director Kash Patel and Article II of the Constitution, which lays out the president's executive powers. The 70-page lawsuit was filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia and names the FBI, Patel, Attorney General Todd Blanche and the Department of Justice as defendants. CBS News has reached out to the Justice Department and FBI for comment. FBI agents executed a search warrant at Mar-a-Lago in August 2022 and allegedly recovered more than 100 documents with classified markings. In 2023, Smith's office indicted Mr. Trump on more than three dozen charges related to his alleged retention of the records and efforts to obstruct the government's attempts to get them back. The charges were ultimately dismissed by the federal judge overseeing the case, who said Smith was unlawfully appointed special counsel. The Justice Department formally abandoned its appeal of the ruling after Mr. Trump won the 2024 election. Thursday's lawsuit cites public comments made by top Justice Department officials and the president directed toward the plaintiffs as evidence the firings were motivated by political animus. For example, Blanche, who was deputy attorney general when the employees were let go, stated that the administration had "cleaned house" at the FBI by firing employees associated with investigations involving the president. The lawsuit contains some new details about the circumstances surrounding the firings. In the case of counterintelligence section chief Jennifer Bacon, she learned she was being let go shortly after an agent named Miles Starr had requested access to the classified investigative files about Plasmic Echo, the codename given to the documents investigation. Starr, the lawsuit said, was a member of Kash Patel's Director's Advisory Team, a group staffed by agents from around the country who support his policy goals. He also was the lead case agent who testified in the since-dismissed indictment charging former FBI Director James Comey with lying to Congress. That testimony later was criticized by a federal magistrate judge, who accused the FBI of numerous missteps, including a failure to filter out potentially privileged materials. On Feb. 23, Starr emailed Assistant Director Roman Rozhavsky to tell him that he urgently needed access to the Plasmic Echo case files, the lawsuit said. "Starr did not explain what he needed, but stated that he was on instructions from Patel to access the case file. Bacon granted him access to all Plasmic Echo files in the FBI's case management system, with the exception of one specific subfile. The files Starr had access to contained the names of all nine Plaintiffs," the lawsuit says. Less than 48 hours later, Bacon and the others were all fired. The lawsuit also suggested that the firings may have been an attempt to distract from negative press about Patel, who was spotted on Feb. 22 at the Olympic Games in Milan "chugging a beer and, in a display of wild immaturity and lack of personal control, flinging alcohol around the U.S. men's hockey team's locker room." A special agent in charge who was assigned to inform former special agent Zach Feldman he was being terminated even surmised that the firing might be "related to the news reports from earlier that day about Director Patel drinking alcohol at the Winter Olympics," the lawsuit said. The military strikes against Iran began on Feb. 28. "This scandal proved politically perilous for Patel: he drew widespread criticism for his conduct, with numerous sources suggesting that his status with President Trump and position as Director of the FBI were in jeopardy as a result," the lawsuit said. On Feb. 25, Patel gave an interview to Reuters in which he disclosed that his phone records and those of White House chief of staff Susie Wiles were subpoenaed as part of Smith's investigations. Eight of the nine plaintiffs were fired the same day, and the ninth was fired the following day. "With over a century of experience among them, these former FBI agents and analysts served our country with honor and distinction as they investigated leaks of national security and defense information, thwarted threats and attacks from our enemies, and responded to critical incidents like the Boston Marathon bombing," attorneys Margaret Donovan, Abbe Lowell and Rebecca Tinio said in a joint statement. "In return for their service, they were fired because they did their jobs, as they always did, to follow the facts and the law without bias or favor." item.title: Guns, F-bombs, fortune cookies. What do wild campaign ads actually say?
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Jennifer Balkcom, a Republican running for Congress in western North Carolina, introduced herself to voters by informing them that her single mom once shot a home intruder. "You break into my house, you're going to get shot," Balkcom's mother says in her twangy mountain accent in a campaign ad posted Sept. 29 on YouTube, which already boasts over 800,000 views. The camera then pans to Balkcom, a 48-year-old state representative, whose mom says she would bring her family's mountain toughness from their house to the House of Representatives as both women hold white coffee cups at a wooden dining room table. The commercial is airing in one of the nation's most competitive congressional races and illustrates the metamorphosis of how campaign ads are produced and consumed during this midterm cycle. Advertisements must be attention grabbing as both parties fight for visibility ahead of Election Day on Nov. 3, political experts, including Travis Ridout, a professor of government and public policy at Washington State University, say. Can you sue over targeted ads? 'Blockbuster' Supreme Court case to decide "I think just the capacity to target nowadays and tailor those messages to specific audiences means it's less (of) the standard generic ad that we're trying to appeal to all voters with," Ridout told USA TODAY. Senator mired in controversy after skipping out on $700 cookie bill Political spending during the 2025-26 election season has already surpassed $10 billion, exceeding the total ad spending in both the 2019-2020 and 2021-2022 election cycles, according to AdImpact Politics, an ad intelligence firm. AdImpact estimates that this year will mark the most expensive election cycle in U.S. history with upward to $11.6 billion in spending. But it's not just the sheer size of the ad buys that stand out. Candidates across the U.S. have used everything from F-bombs to fortune cookies to help boost their own prospects. Wisconsin state Rep. Steve Doyle even held a pet alpaca: "Please, don't fall for emotional appeals. Oh, and this is my baby alpaca, Pasta. She hopes you'll vote for me!" he joked. Meanwhile, former President Barack Obama cut ads to support a slate of Democratic candidates while some Republicans are using their own spots to seek distance from President Donald Trump , who faces sinking approval ratings . Viral F-bombs help flip fates in Illinois In 2024, Cameron Shelton , a political science professor at Claremont McKenna College in California, found in his research that campaign ads confirm previously held biases . "They're usually just sort of, 'How can I activate latent beliefs that somebody already has with very, very simple language and simple images?'" Shelton told USA TODAY. Illinois Lt. Gov. Juliana Stratton was struggling to break out from second place in February in an expensive, bitter Democratic primary to succeed Sen. Dick Durbin, the No. 2 to Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer. Advisor Kaitlin Fahey , the CEO at Chicago-based Magnify Strategies political consulting firm, said Stratton had "one shot" to set herself apart from her opponents, Reps. Raja Krishnamoorthi and Robin Kelly. The Senate races in reliably blue states like Illinois and nearby Minnesota may be sleepier than contests in Michigan or Texas, but the Democratic primaries were no less cutthroat. Krishnamoorthi touted a massive war chest, including financial support from cryptocurrency PACs, while Kelly, a fellow Black woman, wielded the endorsement of the influential Congressional Black Caucus. Then Stratton's "f Trump" ad went viral on X and helped her break out of the congested race. Her Black dad couldn't go to Capitol. She could be a US senator Trump's Midway Blitz immigration enforcement operations in Chicago had left a sour taste in the mouths of many Democratic primary voters – so Stratton's campaign released the profanity-laced spot in which several voters say " f--- Trump , vote Julianna" directly to the camera. "They said it, not me," Stratton then quips, before pledging to stand up to the president. The 30-second video ends with one last " f--- Trump " from Illinois Sen. Tammy Duckworth, and a final "vote Julianna" by Gov. JB Pritzker. The Stratton apparatus knew the profanity-laced ad would make waves, and ruffle feathers, but it was ultimately successful, Fahey said. "We also wanted to raise money off of it. We wanted to earn media attention," Fahey said of the viral video. The ad garnered over 1.6 million all-time views on X. Fahey said her team also wanted the ad to shine more light on the safely blue race but noted that the campaign used other vehicles to discuss Stratton's core policy priorities. While it's impossible to attribute a campaign's success to a single variable, Stratton went on to best Krishnamoorthi by seven points and Kelly by 22. Political food fights At least one Republican adopted a similar bold strategy. In July, Sen. Marsha Blackburn, R-Tennessee, released a controversial ad when she faced an unexpectedly competitive field of primary opponents to replace Gov. Bill Lee. The two-term senator's gubernatorial campaign video featured Blackburn at a Chinese restaurant, surrounded by bottles of soy sauce and fortune cookies wrapped in plastic packaging. "How hard am I going to crack down on China?" Blackburn says, flanked by red booths. "Well, here's a clue." The 74-year-old lawmaker then smashed a series of fortune cookies over a menu while grimacing. A piece of fortune cookie paper read, "MARSHA BLACKBURN WILL FIGHT TO PROTECT TENNESSEE LAND FROM CHINA." Blackburn won the Aug. 6 primary by 10 points over her closest challenger. Swing-state candidates look for broad appeal As candidates in red and blue races double down on appealing to their base, candidates in competitive general election races are aiming to show their independence. Pennsylvania's first-term Rep. Rob Bresnahan is defending a seat he won by less than two points in 2024 in a race rated "toss-up" by the nonpartisan Cook Political Report, which ranks political matchups across the country. (Balkcom, whose mom shot the intruder, faces Jamie Ager in a similar contest.) He caught a bologna chub like a football in a new ad before slamming the meat log down on a kitchen island seemingly pulled straight out of ABC's 2000s suburban drama "Desperate Housewives." "Paige Cognetti and her allies are full of baloney," Bresnahan says, referring to his Democratic opponent, the mayor of Joe Biden 's hometown, Scranton. "Spending millions to paint me as something I am not." In Iowa's toss-up Senate race, Rep. Ashley Hinson is creating space between herself and Trump – despite serving as a longtime surrogate – as she vies for the seat held by retiring Sen. Joni Ernst. Ernst herself starred in a famous campaign commercial, "Squeal," in her first 2014 run for Senate in which she vowed to "make 'em squeal" after telling voters how she grew up castrating hogs . In mid-September, Hinson's campaign released an ad featuring the congresswoman seated in a movie theater. "It used to be that reaching across the aisle wasn't just OK, it was expected," Hinson says, as she handed over a bucket of popcorn across a theater aisle. Monadnock Strategies founder Jesse Hunt, the former communications director at the Republican Governors Association, said campaigns target whatever group they need to win. Democrat Josh Turek leads key Iowa Senate race, new poll shows Sometimes, candidates woo base voters, Hunt said, and other times they seek support from independents like in Hinson's case. "This might sound cliche, but it's all about what each campaign team believes is its winning coalition," Hunt said. Hoops with Obama Hinson's Democratic opponent, state Rep. Josh Turek, is running ads featuring Obama, who endorsed him in a basketball-themed July video . Obama, a noted basketball fan, shared his support for Turek, a two-time Paralympian in wheelchair basketball at the 2016 and 2020 Summer Games. "Now, the ball's in your court," Obama says to Iowans. Obama cut ads in October for a large slate of Democratic candidates in contentious races. He endorsed Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro for governor as well as Colorado's Phil Weiser, Wisconsin's David Crowley and Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia who are competing in open gubernatorial contests. He also endorsed Stratton, Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and Maine's Troy Jackson for Senate. 'I think most politicians are full of...' In a swing district Trump won, one Democratic member of Congress is hoping to reuse unique tactics to distinguish her brand. In 2024, Democratic state Sen. Kristen McDonald Rivet ran against Paul Junge in Michigan's 8th District, which became friendlier to Republicans after it was redrawn in 2023. Now a congresswoman, Rivet enlisted the help of Declaration Media Group , a firm founded by Obama creative alumni who worked on successful battleground races in 2018 and 2020. The Declaration team is again working with Rivet to win re-election in a district that includes Flint. The House member returned to a bar she filmed at during her first bid for Congress in a new ad. "Two years ago, I sat right here and I told you this: 'I think most politicians are full of s---.' It's way worse than I thought," Rivet says. "I approve this message because you deserve better than what you've been getting. I'm working hard to fix that," she adds while holding up a beer glass. A YouTube version posted Oct. 7 has nearly 1 million views . Declaration consultants, including co-founder AJ Lenar, utilized Rivet's background in 2024 to separate her from national Democrats including then-President Joe Biden and Vice President Kamala Harris, who lost Michigan to Trump. Last cycle, Lenar produced an ad where Rivet's husband threw himself out of a car. In the spot, the legislator obsesses over tax cuts on a neighborhood drive, so Joseph Rivet unbuckles his seatbelt and flings himself from the passenger seat of a red Chevrolet Impala. "We knew that district was turning against us demographically, politically, right? And we just felt like we needed to do something that would make her stand out," Lenar told USA TODAY. On Election Day, Rivet won by nearly 7 points while Trump prevailed over Harris by two percentage points in the district. In an upcoming ad, Rivet's spouse will again reprise his role as sidekick – this time, Declaration applied special effects to set his hands on fire. In the original bar spot , Declaration leaned into long held beliefs about sharing brews with officeholders. "They say politics comes down to who you want to have a beer with, so here goes," Rivet says. El-Sayed, Rogers clash: 4 takeaways from the Michigan Senate debate Rivet, who used to run Michigan Head Start, also explains her biography: the lawmaker has six kids. "I know, that's a lot," she says. "Now in the State Senate, I'm fighting to lower drug prices and housing costs and I helped pass the largest tax cut in state history." "I root for the Lions, I hate Ohio and I think most politicians are full of s---," Rivet says. A beer glass slid into her right hand before she hoisted it up and said "Cheers!" An ad standoff in Texas Over 1,000 miles away from mid-Michigan, arguably no race has sparked more conversations about campaign advertising this cycle than the Texas Senate battle. The Lone Star contest has been contentious since before the respective spring primaries determined Democratic state Rep. James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton, the Texas attorney general, would become their parties' nominees. Talarico released an opening ad standing on a rusted pickup truck, surrounded by dozens of people in front of a church. "The biggest divide in our country is not left vs. right, it's top vs. bottom," the Presbyterian seminarian says to cheers. Rep. Jasmine Crockett, a two-term Dallas area congresswoman who also competed in the primaries, shared an announcement video in which she stares to the side as audio of Trump insulting her plays. The contrasting ads stoked online narratives about both candidates – one of which was that Talarico was a man of the people while Crockett was more self-serving. Crockett lost the Senate primary to Talarico, her pre-congressional colleague in the statehouse, in March. Then Talarico's campaign produced several ads to underscore Paxton's ethical dilemmas after Paxton prevailed in a May primary runoff over incumbent Sen. John Cornyn. In one August video, Talarico seized on Paxton taking a $1,000 Montblanc pen from a different man, lawyer Joe Joplin, in 2013 at the Collin County Courthouse. The ad featured security footage ... and an endorsement from Joplin, the pen's owner. Brandon Rottinghaus , a political science professor at the University of Houston, said Talarico's faith-based message has given his candidacy a distinctive identity. Talarico's campaign, Rottinghaus said, has cast him as a centrist who can appeal beyond the Democrats' national brand. "He's able to present himself as somebody who's more moderate in a world that's very polarizing," Rottinghaus told USA TODAY. Paxton is currently and very publicly estranged from his wife, state Sen. Angela Paxton. Recently, she starred in an early October ad that encouraged Republicans to vote red down the ticket. Paxton's camp fought back, too. Their daughter, Mattie Hayworth Paxton, has appeared in multiple ads presenting her dad as a devoted father. Texas is known for its uncertain terrain with its wetlands and deep canyons. The race's landscape is rough, too. Rottinghaus said a win by Talarico could upend ideas about electability. He would be the first Texas Democrat to win a Senate seat since Lloyd Bentsen in 1988. But his videos won't matter as much as votes on Nov. 3. This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Guns, F-bombs, fortune cookies. What do wild campaign ads actually say? item.title: Ukraine resumes strikes on Russian refineries as Zelensky says 'we're done' with truce
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Daniel Flynn and Max Hunder KYIV, Oct 15 (Reuters) - Ukraine struck a Russian oil refinery on Thursday, after President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said Kyiv was "done" supporting a ceasefire on energy targets announced by US President Donald Trump and ignored by Russia. Since Trump's surprise announcement on Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to halt attacks on energy, Kyiv had suspended attacks on Russian refineries, which Trump blames for raising diesel ‌prices on global markets. But in the days that followed, Russia rained down deadly missile and drone strikes, including on energy targets such as power stations, knocking out power to hundreds of thousands of people. In an interview ‌with the Financial Times published on Thursday, Zelenskiy said Ukraine's patience had run out. "The block (on attacking refineries) is out. We're done," he told the newspaper. Zelenskiy also made clear he believed that changes in the capability of the military version of SpaceX's Starlink receptors this week, which have curbed Ukraine's ability to ​use them to pilot its drones, were a policy decision. "It was not a technical problem, it was the will," he told the FT. In a social media post overnight, SpaceX boss Elon Musk said usage of the military version of Starlink, known as Starshield, was ultimately up to Trump, as president of the United States. "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," Musk wrote. BIGGEST RIFT WITH WASHINGTON OF THE WAR By effectively walking away from Trump's demand that Ukraine halt attacks on refineries, Zelenskiy risks deepening the biggest rift between Kyiv and Washington since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Although Trump has described the ceasefire as a requirement for both Moscow and Kyiv, his public comments have ‌focused mainly on Ukraine's attacks on Russian refineries, which he said over the weekend ⁠had "damn well better stop". Trump has long had a testy relationship with Zelenskiy and berated him in the White House in February 2025. But his sharp turn against Kyiv in recent days has little precedent. He first angered Ukraine last week by abruptly lifting sanctions on Russian diesel, and then called on Ukraine to replace Zelenskiy. Ukrainians worry that the rift could have severe consequences on the ⁠battlefield, where the Ukrainian military still depends on technology provided by Washington. Over the past several days, Ukrainian officials have reported that they have not received the usual warnings from Western allies about incoming Russian missiles, which rely on US satellite detectors. Trump has denied withholding intelligence. Zelenskiy said the failure to provide the warnings had been presented to Kyiv as a technical glitch. At the same time, military-grade Starlink receptors have stopped working in Ukraine when mounted on fast-moving objects, interfering with the performance of Ukrainian drones that rely on them for onboard guidance ​systems ​over Ukrainian territory. A source in Ukraine's defence ministry said on Thursday that the receptors were now working when in motion, but only at speeds ​of up to 100 miles per hour (160 kph). Ukrainian officials have said that is too ‌slow for mid-range attack missions and interceptor drones that defend against Russian drones. REFINERY SUPPLYING MOSCOW HIT Ukraine has been using its long-range drones to target Russian refineries and logistics in recent months, which it says is its only answer to nearly five years of relentless Russian bombardment. The attacks have caused fuel shortages in Russia. Trump, under pressure to lower fuel prices, especially for diesel which has reached record highs since he launched a war against Iran in February, says the Ukrainian attacks are driving up global prices. Ukraine's latest target was a refinery in the Ryazan region southeast of Moscow, which is owned by state oil major Rosneft and accounts for nearly 5% of Russia's refinery throughput, helping supply the capital. Regional governor Pavel Malkov said in a post on Telegram that a major Ukrainian drone attack had caused a fire at the refinery. Damage was being assessed and emergency services were at the scene. A Ukrainian official confirmed that Ukraine had hit a Russian refinery overnight in response to Moscow's heavy ballistic ‌missile and drone attacks this week that violated the energy truce. In the latest attacks on Ukraine, three people were killed and six wounded ​in the central region of Kirovohrad overnight, as Russia launched more than 500 drones. State-owned energy company Naftogaz said a gas extraction facility in ​Poltava was damaged and operations were suspended. The Kremlin said on Thursday that Ukraine's targeting of Russian energy infrastructure ran ​counter to US peace efforts. It said earlier this week that the scope of the energy ceasefire had never been determined and work was still ongoing to do so. BREAKDOWN IN RELATIONS In the FT ‌interview, Zelenskiy criticised Washington's eagerness to strike business deals with Moscow and Trump's apparent admiration ​for Russia's Vladimir Putin. The rift has raised concern in Kyiv and ​European capitals about the heavy reliance in Ukraine on US intelligence and technology. Under Trump, Washington has already halted weapons supplies to Ukraine while allowing its European allies to continue buying US arms on Kyiv's behalf. But Europe has no ready-made alternatives to Starlink, or to US satellite systems used to detect Russian missile launches. Zelenskiy has said that Ukrainian military officials had been warned by US counterparts that Washington would block intelligence unless they halted strikes on ​Russian energy infrastructure. Asked whether Ukraine would be open to halting energy strikes as a way ‌of repairing relations with the White House, Zelenskiy told the newspaper he could agree only if in return he were given more US-made Patriot interceptors, calling it the "minimum" that would be acceptable. Ukraine's navy said on ​Thursday it had destroyed six Russian Su-34M military aircraft in an overnight strike on the Borisoglebsk airfield in Russia's Voronezh region. The navy said on Telegram it used its Neptune coastal missile system in ​the attack. item.title: Wholesale inflation jumped last month by most in 4 years as gas prices soared
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Wholesale prices in September rose to their highest level in nearly four years, largely propelled by higher energy prices. The sharp increase stokes concerns that inflation could broaden and keep the Federal Reserve on watch for further rate hikes. The Producer Price Index (PPI) for final demand, which measures the prices that factories, farmers, and producers charge for their finished goods and services, rose 6.3% last month, the largest increase since December 2022. The data trounced expectations for a 5.4% rise. On a "core" basis, excluding food and energy, PPI jumped 0.7% month over month in September, handily higher than market expectations of 0.3%. On a year-over-year basis, this core measure jumped 5.0%, up from 4.7% previously "With a second day in a row of higher-than-expected inflation numbers , it seems the Fed will have no choice but to raise rates again this year," said Chris Zaccarelli, chief investment officer for Northlight Asset Management. "While we don't expect them to raise rates later this month because it is so close to the mid-term election , we do think that they will increase the Fed Funds rate another 25 bps in December," Zaccarelli added. Half of the September increase in the index for final demand goods can be traced to gasoline prices, which jumped 20.3%. In contrast, prices for chicken eggs dropped 39.7%. Read more: How to protect your savings against inflation Looking into the supply chain, the increases in the price of goods sold by one business to another were broad-based, with the index for processed goods rising 2.5%, prices for unprocessed goods moving up 8.4%, and the index for services advancing 0.9%. The index for processed goods sold to other businesses rose 2.5%, the largest rise since jumping 2.8% in May — with most of the increase due to a 10% spike in energy prices. Nearly half of the rise in processed goods sold to other businesses is attributable to a 21% increase in diesel fuel prices . Wholesale prices act as an early-warning pipeline for inflation. If the prices of these input goods rise, manufacturers could pass those higher costs down to consumers later. Yahoo Finance In the Fed's Beige Book, released Wednesday, four districts reported that the pace of price increases has picked up since September. Higher oil prices permeated all 12 Fed districts. Companies reported elevated diesel prices and noted that fuel surcharges were passing on increased costs throughout the supply chain. Businesses in multiple districts also noted continued price pressure from other commodities, tariffs, and insurance. Consumer-facing companies said their profit margins have tightened as price-sensitive customers continue to resist price hikes. Businesses are managing their margins with selective price hikes, targeted incentives, and menu changes that reduce their costs. The reading on wholesale prices for September comes a day after consumer prices also surprised to the upside. The Consumer Price Index rose 3.7% in September, compared with expectations for 3.6%, and an acceleration from 3.4% in August. Month-over-month prices rose 0.6%, versus expectations for 0.5%. Stripping out volatile food and energy prices — the way the Fed likes to scrutinize underlying inflation — CPI rose 0.3% month over month, compared with expectations for 0.2%, holding the same level as August. The year-over-year rate was 2.6%, compared with expectations for 2.5%, and up from 2.4% in August. Analysts will use PPI and CPI to back into the Fed's preferred inflation gauge – the core Personal Consumption Expenditures index. Stephen Brown, an economist at Capital Economics, estimates that core PCE rose 0.35% in September. "That makes an October rate hike a bit more likely, with the FOMC's decision coming down to developments in broader financial conditions in the next couple of weeks and whether Fed officials are happier to surprise the market under Chair Kevin Warsh than has typically been the case," Brown said. A motorist fills up the tank at a gas station in Riverwoods, Ill., on Oct. 14, 2026. (AP Photo/Nam Y. Huh) AP Photo/Nam Y. Huh On Thursday morning, markets were still pricing in only about a 30% chance of the Fed hiking rates in less than two weeks, with a better chance of a hike in December. Investors appear to be taking cues from guidance given earlier this month from Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson and New York Fed president John Williams, who have tempered expectations for a rate hike later this month. Both struck a more cautious tone than several of their colleagues, acknowledging that inflation has remained too high, but warning that the central bank should take time to watch and assess whether inflation will come down in a timely manner. Williams told Bloomberg on Tuesday that he still sees one more interest rate hike as appropriate this year, but doesn't believe the central bank will need to raise rates again in 2027. The minutes from the September meeting read that most participants assessed that another increase in the target range for the federal funds rate would likely be appropriate by year-end. Chicago Fed president Austan Goolsbee told Yahoo Finance on Wednesday that hotter-than-expected September consumer inflation was "discouraging" but suggested that he wants to wait for more data before further raising interest rates. He said core inflation remaining as high as it is now would not be "acceptable" nor "compatible with the Fed target, and our policy needs to address that." At Yahoo Finance, she covers the Federal Reserve, Congress, the White House, the Treasury, the SEC, the economy, cryptocurrencies, and the intersection of Washington policy with finance. item.title: U.S. reportedly weighs using its most powerful non-nuclear bomb against Iran
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb (MOAB) weapon at Eglin Air Force Base, Florida, on March 11, 2003. - Department of Defense/Getty Images/File The US military has developed new strike plans that include potentially using the so-called “mother of all bombs” to target Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites should President Donald Trump give the order to resume combat operations either before or after the midterm elections, according to multiple US officials familiar with the matter. Using the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb or MOAB, the largest non-nuclear bomb in the US arsenal, for the first time in the conflict with Iran would mark a notable escalation, even though there are doubts over how effective it would be in accomplishing any of Trump’s stated strategic objectives or tipping the balance of the war, multiple sources familiar with internal military planning discussions about potentially deploying the weapon said. Trump is facing pressure to bring an end to the deeply unpopular war — as Republicans brace for potential political backlash from voters in the upcoming midterm elections and there is little indication the two countries are close to a negotiated resolution after more than six months of US bombing. While the US military continues to provide Trump with options for potential strikes against outstanding Iranian targets, some officials continue to privately question whether the White House has a strategy that incorporates those plans in a way that could actually end the war — something only the president has the power to do. For months, Trump and his advisers have discussed options that could act as a “definitive” end to the war, at least from a messaging point of view, aware of how unpopular the conflict has become among Americans. While some administration figures have characterized the war as essentially won, Trump has been more guarded in recent remarks, stopping short of declaring victory and saying the US still has unfinished business in the country. Behind the scenes, Trump has also cast doubt on some outside allies who have encouraged him to simply bring US troops home and move on. Doing so, Trump has argued, would look like defeat. Over the course of the last several weeks, White House advisers have held meetings to discuss various options for Iran. While Trump announced publicly that he would not take new actions before the midterms, several advisers said privately they didn’t know whether that statement was definitive or could change before Election Day. Trump has ordered the military to develop additional strike packages against Iranian targets that include “a lot of energy infrastructure” and the potential use of a MOAB, one of the sources told CNN. The same source said the phrasing used was that this attack would come “prior to US retrograde in CENTCOM AOR (area of responsibility),” indicating the administration could launch the additional strikes, attempt to declare victory and quickly pull everyone out. A second source told CNN that military plans for striking Iranian nuclear sites, including Pickaxe Mountain , also explicitly call for using the MOAB. In recent months, Trump has repeatedly threatened to strike Pickaxe, where the US and Israel believe Tehran has stored components of its nuclear program, even after pausing full combat operations earlier this year, and Trump continues to emphasize that his goal is to ensure Iran never obtains a nuclear weapon. Doubts MOAB would be effective Another US official noted that when the military plans, it develops a menu of options for policymakers that range from the high-end to low-end. Higher-end targets, including those that are located deep underground, require bigger bombs, and the MOAB is the biggest, the official added. But there are questions around whether the MOAB would be an effective munition to use against Iran’s nuclear facilities and other sites that are located deep underground. While the GPS-guided bomb is capable of destroying an area equivalent to nine city blocks, it likely lacks the capability to penetrate deep enough under the surface to destroy the suspected nuclear facilities at Pickaxe, which is believed to be fortified by layers of granite, and other remaining Iranian nuclear sites, sources said. The GBU-43/B, also known as the Massive Ordnance Air Blast, detonates during a test at Eglain Air Force Base, Florida, on November 21, 2003. - US Air Force/Handout/Reuters “The MOAB is a massive information operation type weapon that is great for huge area clearance but not much else,” a third source familiar with military planning discussions around Iran told CNN. “It is definitely not designed as a deep penetration warhead.” If used, the MOAB would have devastating effects on the area that it impacts but likely only at the surface level, the sources noted. And the bomb’s massive blast radius would almost certainly raise concerns about the prospect of civilian casualties — particularly if it is used to target Iranian infrastructure targets located near populated areas and in close proximity to non-military sites. Still, Trump could opt to use the MOAB as a psychological weapon at a time when the Iranian regime appears dug in and unwilling to bend to his diplomatic demands. While US officials warn that deploying it is unlikely to force Iran’s capitulation or achieve a strategic military victory — it could provide Trump with an additional option, short of restarting full combat operations, to alter the conflict’s current status quo. “POTUS has unfortunately put himself in a situation where he is almost compelled to do something and, without the ammunition designed to penetrate that level … you have to look at psychological effects for which the MOAB is well-equipped,” the third source familiar with recent planning discussions added. Many within the administration as well as outside analysts agree that the only way to decisively defeat Iran would be through a major operation involving ground troops, a commitment that could potentially cost thousands of American lives. The Pentagon considers all scenarios, so those plans exist, but as of now no one in the administration is arguing for such drastic action. Trump has indicated he has little interest in putting US boots on the ground in Iran but his desire to end the conflict as soon as possible presents a political dilemma for a president who is keenly aware of how unpopular the war has become yet has been unable to secure a diplomatic agreement that would bring it to a close. Top Trump administration officials and military planners have been focused, for weeks, on finding an off-ramp that gives Trump a “symbolic” win — at minimum — he can try to sell to the American people without preventing a potential diplomatic breakthrough, starting with an agreement to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, CNN has reported. A fourth source familiar with the Pentagon’s recent planning discussions on Iran told CNN that military officials had developed some options that would amount to a “fireworks show,” with the goal of providing Trump an off-ramp from the conflict even if those strikes fail to accomplish his stated goals for starting the war in the first place. And despite Trump’s recent pledge to hold off on launching additional strikes before the midterms, the US military already appears to be preparing for potential Iranian retaliation should the president give the go-order. The next turnover of US troops deployed to CENTCOM is also expected to take place within the next few weeks, according to a fifth source, a US official who acknowledged it is possible some of the personnel who rotate out of the region, may not be replaced by fresh service members. Asked about the plans, a White House official told CNN that they do not comment on sensitive military plans that may or may not exist, adding “President Trump keeps all options on the table to ensure that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon.” In response to CNN’s request for comment, a Pentagon official said: “The Department of War plans for a wide range of operational scenarios to execute Presidential and Secretary‑level direction and to ensure mission success in any operational environment.” MOAB developed for ‘psychological operations’ Developed during the Iraq War, the MOAB is an air blast-type warhead that explodes before hitting the ground to project a massive explosion from all sides. During the final stages of testing in 2003 , military officials told CNN the MOAB was mainly conceived as a weapon employed for “psychological operations.” Military officials said then they hoped such a huge blast would rattle Iraqi troops and pressure them into surrendering or not even fighting. As originally conceived, the MOAB was to be used against large formations of troops and equipment or hardened above-ground bunkers. The target set has been expanded to include targets buried under softer surfaces, such as caves or tunnels. Trump was the first US president to deploy the MOAB, during his first term when he authorized the military to use its most powerful non-nuclear bomb on ISIS positions in Afghanistan in 2017. unknown content item - That strike targeted a network of fortified underground tunnels that ISIS had been using to stage attacks on government forces — killing 36 ISIS fighters, Afghan officials said. The blast destroyed three underground tunnels as well as weapons and ammunition, but no civilians were hurt, Afghan and US officials added at the time. At the time, the bombing marked a dramatic change in attitude for Trump , who advocated an isolationist, “America first” foreign policy during his first election campaign. Following the 2017 strike, US military officials were pressed on whether the 21,600-pound bomb was necessary for that particular target and would likely face similar questions if the munition is deployed against Iran. item.title: Trump admin. sues California over alleged noncitizens on state's voter rolls
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Andrew Goudsward and Luc Cohen WASHINGTON, Oct 15 (Reuters) - The US Justice Department sued California on Thursday, asking a federal judge to block the state from counting mail ballots for the November 3 midterm elections from more than 20,000 voters the Trump administration alleges are ‌likely noncitizens. The lawsuit marks the latest effort by President Donald Trump's administration to boost the federal government's role in elections ahead of the ‌midterms, with his Republican Party locked in a tight battle to retain control of both houses of Congress. The US Constitution assigns the responsibility of administering elections to individual states, though the federal government ​has some oversight role. Trump has repeatedly claimed that voting by noncitizens - which is illegal - is widespread, despite multiple studies showing it is rare. A Reuters investigation published in July found that just 129 people had been prosecuted for noncitizen voting since the statute criminalizing it passed in 1996. The Justice Department has ramped up such prosecutions in recent months. In the lawsuit filed in federal court in Los Angeles, the Justice Department sought a court order preventing California from "tabulating in federal elections vote-by-mail ballots received" ‌from more than 20,000 voters until their immigration status is ⁠verified. Reuters previously reported that the department sent California a letter giving it a 48-hour deadline on Tuesday to review the list of alleged noncitizen voters. The list was provided on a thumb drive. CALIFORNIA SAYS DOJ SEEKS CHAOS The lawsuit marks an escalation ⁠in the federal government's pressure on state election officials over alleged noncitizen voting. The Justice Department has warned election officials in all 50 states that they could face criminal prosecution if they knowingly allowed noncitizens to remain on their voter rolls or cast ballots. It has sued 30 states and Washington DC for refusing to provide complete voter rolls including voters' ​sensitive ​personal data, but has lost 26 of those cases so far without winning one. In Thursday's ​lawsuit against California, the Justice Department said the Department of Homeland ‌Security had identified the 20,000 alleged noncitizens by comparing voter rolls to its own internal databases. Voting rights activists have expressed concern that many citizens who are naturalized could be wrongly flagged as noncitizens due to outdated DHS data. California Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder Dean Logan, who were named as defendants in the lawsuit, did not immediately respond to requests for comment. In a statement on Wednesday about the letter, Weber said California's safeguards against noncitizen voting were robust. "The USDOJ's relentless efforts to unlawfully gain access to states' protected voter data and purge voter rolls serve only to cause chaos and fuel public distrust in ‌our elections," Weber said. NONCITIZENS HAVE BEEN REGISTERED THROUGH ERRORS Though states may have added more than ​30,000 noncitizens to their voter rolls since 2000 due to software glitches and clerical errors, Reuters ​found in September, it was unclear how many had cast a ballot. ​Experts said the numbers were too small relative to the country’s 170 million registered voters to affect elections. Rick Hasen, a law ‌professor at the University of California, Los Angeles, and an expert ​on election law, said the DOJ’s request ​would potentially cause California to violate a federal law barring states from conducting mass purges of voter rolls within 90 days of an election. The Trump administration has argued in another case that such restrictions should not apply to removal of noncitizens because they were not legally authorized to ​register in the first place. Hasen said the DOJ lawsuit would ‌likely face legal hurdles. “The federal government doesn’t have any business directly telling states what ballots they can or cannot send out or ​not count,” he said. “I just don’t see the federal authority to do that over a state.” (Reporting by Andrew Goudsward in Washington and Luc ​Cohen in New York; Editing by Michelle Nichols, Matthew Lewis and David Gregorio) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/doj-sues-california-block-votes-171601356.html

item.title: GOP questions the accuracy of polling leading up to the midterms
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Republicans nervous about the midterms are increasingly turning to the same salve: The polling will be wrong. They aren't suggesting Republicans will have a good night come Nov. 3 — or that the party will hold the House. But they're clinging to the possibility that it could be a typically bad midterm year reminiscent of 2022, when polls projected Democrats would be pummeled, only for those predictions to fall short. It's happened in other cycles, too, they note. President Donald Trump outperformed final polling averages in all seven swing states in 2024 and defied the national polls in 2016 as well. This story is based on conversations with more than a dozen people, including veteran GOP operatives, pollsters, strategists working on battleground races and national party officials. Most conceded the national environment is bad for Republicans and has only gotten worse over the last few months. But even a small sampling error, they say, could completely change how election night turns out for the GOP. "Part of the challenge here is polling still has not figured out how to model Republican voters who either don't answer the phone or just aren't really interested in polling, and so I do think that the Senate map across the board, there's more reason to doubt the polls than you would guess by seeing how both media and Democrats are treating this," said Matt Whitlock, a GOP strategist and former National Republican Senatorial Committee senior adviser. Republicans' growing reliance on bad polling to ease their pain reflects the dour mood gripping the party. With less than three weeks until Election Day, Republicans are increasingly pessimistic about their prospects, as persistent inflation, high prices on everyday items, elevated mortgage rates and a lingering war in the Middle East hamper campaigns. On Wednesday, the Labor Department reported inflation accelerated more than expected in September driven by soaring gas prices, the latest blow to Republicans who are facing voters' ire over cost-of-living concerns. And this week, top Republican super PACs aligned with Trump and congressional Republican leadership pulled money from a handful of GOP House members seeking reelection. Senior House Republicans have privately concluded that the chamber is all but gone and party leaders are shifting resources to save the Senate. Both the White House and RNC said polls have sold short GOP support. White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said "underestimating" Trump and his administration "have proven the experts and pollsters wrong every single time," while RNC national press secretary Natalie Baldassarre added that "bed-wetting strategists who aren't in the game always take the bait." "Republicans are united in exposing the far-left's extreme agenda and will leave it all on the table to defy history in November," she said. But the polling, like the economic headwinds, has only worsened in recent weeks. Democrats hold a roughly 9-point national lead on the generic congressional ballot, up from about 6.5 points around Labor Day. That's slightly wider than the Democrats' lead at this point in 2018, when the party rode a blue wave to a 41-seat gain in the House. Senate seats in GOP strongholds such as Texas, Alaska, Iowa and Kansas are in play, as independent voters sour on the president and his policies. Still, GOP strategist Colin Reed said the polling industry is "very much in transition" and that making predictions in the Trump era is a "risky gambit." GOP pollster Patrick Ruffini, co-founder of Echelon Insights, found that in three Midwestern states — Iowa, Michigan and Ohio — 93 percent of Senate polls overestimated the Democratic candidate's performance. In both midterm and presidential election years, polls a month out from the election were off by an average of more than 6 points in Democrats' favor. "We can get the environment right, but the map wrong," Ruffini said. "Even if you buy this idea of a Democratic wave, a good Democratic year, a very solidly pro-Democratic environment, we should be concerned about the track record of the polls — particularly in some of these red states where there have been some pretty large misses, and especially in the Midwest." Part of the challenge is no one knows what the midterm electorate will look like, making it hard to know if the polling is accurate. A White House official, who like others in this story was granted anonymity to speak candidly, said they didn't think that Black voters would show up for Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, but it's unclear whether that means they vote for Republican Mike Rogers — or just stay home. "There is a narrative building process in all of these different polls," the official said, adding that "it's different in every state. There's not a one size fits all. Whenever you look at which poll is overweighting which subset of voters, they're all over the place." That's partly why Trump is appearing in red states — to shape the electorate and make sure it's reflective of the MAGA coalition that carried him to victory in 2024. Multiple GOP strategists pointed to 2022 when Democrats outperformed expectations and held the Senate, even as they lost the House. The Biden White House, even with the loss of the lower chamber, took a victory lap, celebrating the better-than-expected election night as a "good day." "Republicans' only hope in '26 is that what happened to us in '22 happens to Democrats in '26," said a GOP strategist working on battleground races. "There's a part of me that thinks there is a scenario where 2022 repeats itself. But if the polling is right … then I think it's setting up to be one of the worst cycles in history for Republicans." Polling over the last decade has struggled to capture Republican voters. The data underestimated Trump's support in 2016, 2020 and 2024, and Republicans argue similar errors could be happening again this cycle, particularly in competitive Senate races. "Polling is getting much more difficult to do," said veteran GOP strategist Karl Rove, adding that if the polls reflect Democratic overperformance "then every one of these races that we're talking about today — Texas, Michigan, Maine, Alaska, Iowa — they're all within the margin of error." An RNC official argued that public polls skew toward Democrats. "It's not to say that the environment's wildly different from what we anticipated it was going to be, which is a tough one in a midterm, which is what history tells you a midterm environment is going to be," the person said. "I think generally speaking, the polls are far more pessimistic than the reality is for Republicans in the midterms." Text polling has skewed the responses because it overpresents young liberal voters and progressives, especially in states that have a large white population, as many of the Great Plains states do, said a second GOP strategist working on competitive midterm races. Pollsters try to balance their samples but can only do so much to correct for that. The strategist also noted that the polling right now reflects a change in the electorate as profound as those seen after Watergate and 9/11. "It would be so historically unprecedented you'd have to presuppose we're staring down the barrel of a generational national trauma that no one is aware of," the strategist said. Adam Wren contributed to this report. This article originally appeared on Politico at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/republicans-last-hope-2026-another-090000613.html

item.title: Trump says he's 'very proud' as he unveils newly renovated White House facade
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
President Donald Trump has shared new images of what he described as the “fully renovated” White House facade, saying extensive restoration work has given the historic building decades of additional life. Trump posted photographs of the South side of the White House to Truth Social early Thursday, highlighting restoration of the exterior as well as a new South Entrance and helipad. “Actual pictures of our fully renovated White House facade, facing South, with the new South Entrance, and Heliport!” Trump wrote. “It had to be done, and I am very proud to be the President who did it!” Trump added. President Donald Trump is seen on the South Lawn of the White House in Washington, D.C., on September 26, 2026. The work comes amid a much broader transformation of the White House complex during Trump’s second term, including work on the North Portico, changes to the Rose Garden and extensive construction on the site of the former East Wing for a new ballroom and military complex. Trump said Thursday that the ballroom and military complex were “on time, and on budget,” describing them as an “unbelievably beautiful addition” to the White House. The project has been the subject of legal challenges and scrutiny over its cost and funding, with the Supreme Court allowing construction to continue in August while litigation over the project proceeds. Newsweek has contacted the White House and National Park Service for further comment. The South Lawn of the White House in Washington, DC, as seen March 20, 2009. What Changed at the White House? Trump’s newly released photographs focus on the South facade, one of the most recognizable views of the White House. The South Portico, with its curved colonnade and Truman Balcony above it, faces the South Lawn and has historically served as an arrival and departure point for presidents and foreign leaders. Trump said the work addressed deterioration to both the building’s exterior walls and decorative architectural features. “Over the years, the facade, both North and South, suffered tremendous wear, tear, and damage,” he wrote. “The exterior walls and ornamentation, both missing and in bad condition, has been fully restored to the Highest Level, giving the White House many decades of additional life!” The president did not provide a detailed breakdown of the restoration work or its cost. Work has also been underway on the White House’s North Portico. The Washington Post reported in September that workers had spent roughly two months repairing the historic columns and strengthening the entrance before coverings surrounding the structure began to be removed. The White House itself dates to the 1790s, although the building has repeatedly been rebuilt, expanded and renovated. The South Portico was constructed during James Monroe’s presidency in the 1820s, while the North Portico was added several years later under Andrew Jackson. The West Wing was constructed during Theodore Roosevelt’s presidency in 1902 and the White House underwent a near-total interior reconstruction during Harry Truman’s presidency between 1948 and 1952. An image posted on Truth Social shows the newly renovated White House facade. Trump’s White House Renovations The facade restoration is part of a series of changes Trump has made to the White House and its grounds, among the most significant being the ballroom and associated East Wing redevelopment. The original East Wing was demolished as the administration moved ahead with plans for a large new ceremonial space and additional security and military infrastructure. Trump initially promoted the ballroom as a privately funded addition designed to give the White House a permanent space for large state events rather than relying on temporary tents. The project has since expanded to include substantial underground security infrastructure and other facilities. In August, the Supreme Court permitted construction to continue while a lawsuit brought by the National Trust for Historic Preservation proceeds. The Court said its ruling did not decide the ultimate legality of the project but found that the government was likely to prevail on its argument that the preservation group lacked standing. Trump has repeatedly said taxpayers will not pay for the ballroom itself. In September, he said the ballroom would cost close to $400 million and was being funded by himself and private companies. Internal contractor documents reported by The Washington Post , however, estimated the wider East Wing project at about $600 million, with approximately $293 million expected from private sources and the remainder associated with government-funded security, military and Executive Residence work. The White House has said those taxpayer-funded costs relate to security and other government functions rather than the ballroom itself. Trump reiterated Thursday that the work remained on schedule. “Likewise, the Ballroom and Military Complex, is on time, and on budget,” he wrote. Trump said the development would be the most significant addition to the White House since the West Wing was constructed. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Tobias Meyjes and Tony Phillips . item.title: Beef prices are soaring — and now meat is a midterm election issue
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
In the midterm elections , meat is on the menu. As Democrats and Republicans argue over high prices and the Iran war , they also are having a food fight over who is the most red-blooded carnivore. The latest example came this week in Mississippi, where Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Scott Colom released a video with a snippet of Cindy Hyde-Smith, the Republican incumbent, saying that if consumers are upset over high beef prices, "you know you have so many proteins to choose from." The video cuts to a man grilling burgers who says, "Pick another protein? I'd rather pick another senator instead." The Mississippi race is somewhat unusual because it is the Democrat hammering the Republican over beef. Elsewhere, Republicans have branded Democrats as vegans or otherwise opposed to meat, trying to show that they are culturally out of step with voters, hostile to local cattle industries or just not manly enough. In Texas, Republicans seized on an old interview in which Democrat James Talarico, the current U.S. Senate nominee, boasted that his campaign at the time for the Texas Statehouse was going vegan. Talarico has since been publicly scarfing down barbecue to rebut allegations that his dietary choices mean he is not a real Texan. Chowing down on barbecue and tacos In Colorado, Republicans have gone after Democratic congressional candidate Manny Rutinel for his activism against meat production and factory farming. In college, he was photographed shirtless with a banner for the People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals around his chest. In 2021, Rutinel founded Climate Refarm, which advocated for cutting down on the use of meat and has signed onto letters advocating for raising taxes on meat and dairy. He also supported a 2024 ballot measure to ban a lamb slaughterhouse in Denver, which failed. Rutinel, 31, is now running against Gabe Evans, the Republican who represents Colorado's 8th Congressional District. The vast swath in the northeastern part of the state is dotted with ranches, dairy farms and meat processing facilities, including the headquarters of beef production titan JBS Swift. Republicans have hammered Rutinel over advocating veganism, to the point that the conservative media group Daily Wire this week released an undercover video of a campaign official saying Rutinel eats meat "as little as possible." Rutinel has made a point of publicly eating steak tacos during the campaign and is backed by the meatpackers' union. "I don't think Coloradans care about what's on my plate," he said in an interview after a recent campaign stop. "I think they care more about being able to afford what's on theirs." Evans said the issue goes beyond Rutinel's meal preferences. "I don't care what he eats personally," Evans said in an interview. "I care that he wants to use the power of the government to make everyone eat that way." High-stakes role for meat in the debate over rising consumer prices Republicans, in the same way, have gone after two other Democrats running for the U.S. House. They are hammering Lindsay James in Iowa's 2nd District, an area filled with hog farms, over a 2020 Facebook post supporting "meatless May," and Amish Shah in Arizona's 1st District for his long-standing vegetarianism and animal rights activism. Also in Iowa, Republican U.S. Senate nominee Rep. Ashley Hinson slammed her opponent, state lawmaker Josh Turek, for opposing a bill banning lab-grown meat from being sold in the state. "He'd rather have meat that comes from a lab than from our family farms," the congresswoman said at a campaign appearance. Democrats have spotlighted meat as well, but mainly as one of the staples that cost more under Trump, squeezing voters' pocketbooks. Trump has tried to lower prices by opening U.S. markets to beef imports, especially from Argentina, which is governed by a close Trump ally. Those moves, however, have angered U.S. producers as prices have remained stubbornly high, creating a potential weakness in Republican-leaning states where Democrats hope to gain ground this year. According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the average pound of ground beef cost $6.79 last month, up from $5.55 in January of 2025, when Trump returned to office. That was the dynamic that Hyde-Smith, a cattle rancher and former Mississippi agriculture commissioner, was addressing in her interview that was clipped in Colom's video. The prosecutor — who also delivers the "pick another senator" line in the spot — is running a long-shot challenge in Mississippi. A spokesman for Hyde-Smith's campaign argued that the Democrats deserve blame for high prices. item.title: FBI investigates suspicious mail sent to Senate and election offices
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — Federal authorities are investigating letters with “suspicious substances” that have been mailed to congressional and election offices nationwide and are urging recipients to treat the mailings as “potentially hazardous.” The investigation by the FBI, U.S. Postal Inspection Service and U.S. Capitol Police was first disclosed in a message from the Senate Sergeant at Arms obtained Thursday by The Associated Press. The notice, sent to Senate offices, said that law enforcement officials were working to intercept any additional letters, but “it is possible that some letters may reach their destinations.” In Congress, the threat appeared limited to the Senate, though the House was monitoring the situation, according to a person familiar with the matter who was not authorized to discuss the investigation publicly. An FBI statement said the bureau and the Postal Inspection Service were "investigating a series of suspicious mailings sent to various addresses nationwide, including Secretary of State offices and their related election offices.” "Some of the letters contained an unknown substance and we are working closely with our law enforcement partners to respond to each incident," the statement read. "We are also working with our partners to identify the individual or individuals responsible for the letters." Mailed packages containing a powdery substance led to the evacuation this week of election offices in at least two states, Louisiana and Oklahoma. The Ohio secretary of state said the Postal Service intercepted a package containing a white powder intended for its office and noted that similar mailings had been sent to election officials in multiple states. Maryland, Mississippi and South Dakota officials on Thursday said their election offices also were targeted by separate mailings but that the letters were intercepted by the Postal Service. News of the letters comes just three weeks before Election Day and is reminiscent of a similar threat in 2023, when election offices in six states received mailings that contained a white powder. In some cases, the incidents disrupted work around local elections. Some of those letters contained threats and traces of the powerful opioid fentanyl, leading some election offices to stock up on the overdose reversal medication naloxone. The National Association of Secretaries of State and the National Association of State Election Directors issued a joint statement condemning what they said were threats against election staff. “Those who administer our elections should never fear for their safety while carrying out their essential duties,” they said in their statement. Deputy Postal Inspector Brendan Donahue told reporters Thursday that “any threat or attack on election officials is unacceptable” and that “we are also working with our partners on identifying the individual or individuals responsible for the letters.” ___ Associated Press writers Scott Bauer in Madison, Wisconsin; Sarah Rankin in Richmond, Virginia; and Nicholas Riccardi in Denver contributed to this report.
